questions.question: A junior engineer asks whether a Docker image and a Docker container are the same object. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the two?
options: An image is a read-only stack of filesystem layers; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of that image with a writable top layer and its own namespaces
An image and a container are two names for the same runtime artifact; the term used depends on whether the artifact is idle or executing
An image is the packaging format used in development while a container is the packaging format used in production; they share no other technical distinction
A container is the on-disk representation stored under /var/lib/docker while an image is the in-memory copy loaded when execution begins
questions.explanation: An image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot; a container is a live instance created from that image with an extra thin writable layer and its own PID/network/mount namespaces. The 'two names for the same thing' answer is wrong because containers add runtime state (writable layer, namespaces, cgroups) that an image lacks. Splitting them by 'dev vs prod' invents a distinction that does not exist — the same image runs everywhere. Claiming the container lives on disk while the image is in memory inverts reality: image layers sit on disk in the graph driver's storage, and only the running process view is loaded into memory.

questions.question: A Dockerfile declares `ENTRYPOINT ["python"]` and `CMD ["app.py"]`. Which instruction supplies the default arguments that are overridden by any command passed to `docker run`?
options: CMD
EXEC
ENTRYPOINT
RUN
questions.explanation: CMD provides default arguments (or a default command) that `docker run image <args>` overrides; combined with ENTRYPOINT it supplies the arguments to that entrypoint. EXEC is not a Dockerfile instruction at all — the exec form refers to the JSON-array syntax used by CMD/ENTRYPOINT, not a separate keyword. ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable and is only replaced by the `--entrypoint` flag, not by a positional arg on `docker run`. RUN executes commands at build time to modify the image and has no effect on what runs when the container starts.

questions.question: An administrator wants an nginx container to detach from the terminal, restart automatically if it crashes, and come back up after the Docker daemon or host restarts. Which `docker run` invocation satisfies all three requirements?
options: docker run --daemon --always-restart nginx
docker run --background --restart=on-failure nginx
docker run -d --restart=always nginx
docker run -d --keep-alive nginx
questions.explanation: `-d` detaches the container from the terminal, and `--restart=always` restarts it on crash and re-starts it whenever the Docker daemon (and therefore the host) comes back up. `--daemon` and `--always-restart` are not real `docker run` flags, so the first option would be rejected by the CLI. `--background` is also invented; `--restart=on-failure` only restarts on non-zero exits and would not bring the container back after a daemon restart on a clean exit. `--keep-alive` is not a real flag and provides neither restart policy nor detach behavior.

questions.question: A shell pipeline must receive only container IDs — one per line, no header, no other columns — so they can be fed to `xargs docker rm`. Which command prints exactly that?
options: docker ps -q
docker list --quiet
docker container show --id-only
docker container ls --ids
questions.explanation: `docker ps -q` (equivalent to `docker container ls -q`) prints only the truncated container IDs, one per line, with no header — exactly what is required for piping into another command. `docker list` is not a valid Docker CLI verb; the command would fail. `docker container show` does not exist either; the correct verbs are `ls` and `inspect`. `--ids` is not a real flag on `docker container ls`; the flag that outputs IDs only is `-q`/`--quiet`.

questions.question: A Docker host has accumulated stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, and unused build cache. Which single command removes all of that categories after a confirmation prompt?
options: docker clean all
docker rm --all && docker rmi --all
docker system prune
docker purge --system
questions.explanation: `docker system prune` removes stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, and the build cache in one confirmed step (add `-a` to also remove unused tagged images, `--volumes` to also drop unused volumes). `docker clean` is not a real Docker subcommand and would be rejected. `--all` is not a valid flag on `docker rm` or `docker rmi`; those commands take explicit ID lists and would also miss networks and build cache. `docker purge` is not a Docker command at all.

questions.question: A repository holds a large `node_modules/`, `.git/`, and log files next to the Dockerfile. `docker build .` currently ships all of them to the daemon as build context. Which mechanism excludes files from being sent to the daemon in the first place?
options: A .dockerignore file at the build-context root
Setting the excluded paths as hidden environment variables at build time
Adding an EXCLUDE instruction to the Dockerfile so those paths are skipped
Blocking the affected paths in the daemon's registry pull policy
questions.explanation: The `.dockerignore` file at the root of the build context tells the CLI which paths to strip before sending the tarball to the daemon, keeping the context small and preventing secrets or huge directories from being uploaded. Environment variables have no bearing on which files are packaged into the build context — they configure processes, not the context filter. There is no EXCLUDE Dockerfile instruction; ignoring context files must happen client-side. The registry pull policy controls how images are fetched from a registry, not what the local CLI sends into a build.

questions.question: A Go service compiles to a 50 MB static binary but the Go toolchain adds 800 MB. Which technique lets a single Dockerfile produce a small runtime image that contains only the compiled binary?
options: Parallel-image builds where multiple FROM instructions each compile a different image concurrently
A multi-stage build where later FROM stages COPY only the artifacts they need from earlier build stages
Cross-platform builds where multiple FROM instructions target different OS/arch pairs simultaneously
Conditional builds where multiple FROM instructions branch on if/else logic during compile
questions.explanation: A multi-stage build uses several FROM directives inside one Dockerfile; the runtime stage starts from a minimal base image and COPYs only the compiled binary out of a heavier build stage, keeping the final image tiny. The 'parallel images' option is wrong because a Dockerfile produces exactly one tagged output image, not one per FROM. Multi-stage is unrelated to cross-platform builds — those use `--platform` and buildx, not FROM chaining. Dockerfiles have no if/else construct; conditional logic must be handled by build args or external tooling, not by FROM.

questions.question: A MySQL container's data must survive container restarts, container removal, daemon restart, and host reboot, and its storage should be managed by Docker rather than pinned to a specific host path. Which storage type fits?
options: The container's own writable layer at /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff
A named Docker volume created with docker volume create
A tmpfs mount targeted at /var/lib/mysql
A bind mount from /tmp on the host into the container
questions.explanation: A named volume is stored under Docker's control, persists independently of any container, and can be reattached to a new container after removal — exactly what a database needs. The writable layer is discarded when the container is removed, so it fails requirement (b). A tmpfs mount lives in RAM and evaporates whenever the container stops, which fails every requirement except restart-in-place. A bind mount to `/tmp` is not Docker-managed and, on most Linux distributions, `/tmp` is cleaned at boot (via systemd-tmpfiles), so the database would be wiped on host reboot.

questions.question: COPY and ADD both place files into an image, and best-practice guidance is to prefer COPY. Which capability does ADD have that COPY does not?
options: ADD sets stricter default file permissions on copied paths than COPY does
The two instructions are functionally identical and ADD has been deprecated
ADD can fetch remote URLs and automatically extract recognized tar archives into the target
ADD copies whole directories whereas COPY handles only individual files
questions.explanation: ADD's extra powers are the two that COPY intentionally omits: fetching content from a remote URL and auto-extracting local tar files at the destination. That implicit behavior is exactly why best practice is to prefer COPY. The permissions claim is false; both instructions honor `--chown`/`--chmod` identically and default to the source's ownership. ADD is not deprecated — Docker keeps it and simply recommends against it. Both COPY and ADD copy directories recursively; the distinction is not files-only vs directories.

questions.question: An operator needs the complete configuration of an image: environment variables, entrypoint, CMD, default user, labels, working directory, and the image's config-blob digest. Which command emits that metadata?
options: docker inspect <image>
docker image history <image>
docker image info <image>
docker image describe <image>
questions.explanation: `docker inspect` (or `docker image inspect`) returns the full JSON metadata blob for an image — including Env, Cmd, Entrypoint, WorkingDir, User, Labels, and layer digests — which is exactly the requested set of fields. `docker image history` lists the sequence of layers with their creating instruction and size, but it does not expose the full config (no ENV list, no default user, no labels). `docker image info` and `docker image describe` are not real Docker CLI verbs; the shell would reject both.

questions.question: By default, `docker run nginx` attaches the new container to a single-host network that uses a Linux bridge plus iptables NAT for outbound traffic and port publishing for inbound. Which built-in network driver provides that behavior?
options: The none driver, which leaves the container with only a loopback interface
The bridge driver, backed by the docker0 Linux bridge and iptables NAT
The overlay driver, which builds a multi-host VXLAN network for Swarm services
The host driver, which shares the host's network namespace with the container
questions.explanation: The bridge driver is Docker's default single-host driver: it plugs each container into the docker0 Linux bridge, gives it a private RFC1918 IP, and uses iptables NAT to reach the internet or publish ports. The none driver removes all connectivity — not the default and not the described behavior. The overlay driver is a multi-host Swarm construct built on VXLAN, not the default per-container network. The host driver shares the host's network namespace entirely, so there is no isolated bridge or NAT — exactly the opposite of what the question describes.

questions.question: Two containers on a user-defined bridge can reach each other by container name (`ping web`), but the same two containers on the default `bridge` network cannot. Why does name resolution work on user-defined bridges but not on the default bridge?
options: User-defined bridges ship with an embedded DNS server that resolves container names; the default bridge does not
The default bridge is IPv6-only, so IPv4-only container names cannot resolve on it
Name resolution between containers requires Docker Compose to be installed
Name-based resolution does work on the default bridge; the operator has simply misconfigured DNS
questions.explanation: User-defined bridges include Docker's embedded DNS resolver (127.0.0.11) that maps container names and aliases to IPs; the default `bridge` network was kept in its legacy behavior and relies on the deprecated `--link` flag or explicit IPs for cross-container discovery. The default bridge is dual-stack when IPv6 is enabled — it is not IPv6-only, and the IPv4/IPv6 distinction is unrelated to name resolution. Compose is not required; it only sets up user-defined networks under the hood. Claiming that resolution 'does work' on the default bridge contradicts documented Docker behavior.

questions.question: A Swarm cluster has replicas of a service spread across three managers and five workers. The replicas must communicate as if they were on the same Layer-2 broadcast domain even though they run on different hosts. Which network driver satisfies that requirement?
options: The host driver, which attaches each container directly to the host network
The overlay driver, which encapsulates traffic between Swarm nodes with VXLAN
A CDN-backed network driver that routes container traffic through an edge PoP
A single-node encrypted network driver scoped to one host at a time
questions.explanation: The overlay driver builds a multi-host virtual L2 network by wrapping frames in VXLAN and sending them between Swarm nodes over the underlay; containers on different hosts see one another as if on the same LAN. The host driver only removes network isolation on a single node and does nothing to bridge separate hosts. There is no CDN-backed built-in network driver; CDNs sit outside the container network model entirely. A single-node encrypted network is a contradiction — Docker does support `--opt encrypted`, but only on overlay networks that already span nodes, not on a per-host driver.

questions.question: An admin wants to bootstrap the very first manager of a new Swarm cluster on the current host: initialize the Raft cluster, generate join tokens for future managers and workers, and become the leader. Which command does this?
options: docker swarm create --advertise-addr <ip>
docker cluster create --mode manager
docker swarm start --manager
docker swarm init [--advertise-addr <ip>]
questions.explanation: `docker swarm init` bootstraps the Swarm on the current node, promotes it to manager and Raft leader, and prints the `docker swarm join --token …` commands for worker and manager nodes; `--advertise-addr` is added when the host has more than one interface. `docker swarm create` and `docker swarm start` are not real subcommands — the create/start verbs exist for services, not the swarm itself. `docker cluster create` is not a Docker CLI verb either; Swarm's bootstrap primitive is spelled `swarm init`.

questions.question: In Docker Swarm terminology, how do a service and a task differ?
options: A service declares desired state — image, replicas, ports, constraints — and a task is one running container instance the scheduler creates to satisfy that state
A task is the persistent Raft record of the workload while the service is a stateless CLI wrapper that only exists during the create-or-update call
A service is defined to run exactly one container, while a task is a scheduling group that bundles multiple replicas of that container together on one node
Service and task are two aliases for the same Swarm object; the label used depends on whether the object is being created, inspected, or scaled
questions.explanation: A service is the declarative unit — image, replica count, networks, constraints, update policy — and the manager decomposes it into tasks, each of which is one scheduled container instance on a specific node. It is the tasks that are ephemeral: when one dies, the manager creates a new task to keep the replica count at the desired level. Persistent Raft state lives on the manager quorum, not inside tasks, so the second option is inverted. A service can have many replicas (or run globally on every node), so 'exactly one container' is wrong. And service and task are two different objects with different subcommands (`docker service`, `docker service ps`), not synonyms.

questions.question: A Swarm service called `webapp` currently runs three replicas and needs to run five. Which command scales it to the new replica count?
options: docker swarm scale webapp 5
docker service resize webapp --replicas=5
docker service update webapp --count=5
docker service scale webapp=5
questions.explanation: `docker service scale webapp=5` sets the replica count; several services can be scaled in one call (`docker service scale a=3 b=5`), and the manager schedules new tasks or terminates surplus ones. `docker swarm scale` is not a real subcommand — scaling is a service operation, not a swarm-level one. `docker service resize` does not exist. `docker service update --count=5` uses the wrong flag; the correct spelling is `--replicas=5`, which is also a valid but less compact alternative to `service scale`.

questions.question: Docker Content Trust (DCT), when enabled via `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`, causes Docker to accept only image tags that carry a valid publisher signature. Which of the following best describes what DCT actually does?
options: Encrypts image layers server-side in the registry so their bytes cannot be read while the image sits at rest between push and pull
Requires the pulling user to complete two-factor authentication (TOTP or WebAuthn) at the CLI before Docker will begin the pull
Uses digital signatures over image manifests (backed by Notary/TUF) so tampering after publication is detected on pull
Scans images for known CVE vulnerabilities and blocks any image that has an unfixed critical or high finding from being pulled or run
questions.explanation: DCT signs image tags with keys managed by Notary (built on The Update Framework); on pull, Docker verifies the signature before accepting the image, so tampering or MITM substitution after publication is caught. DCT does not encrypt layers — registries and clients can still see the layer bytes, they simply verify the signature. DCT does not add 2FA on the user account; it authenticates the publisher, not the pulling user. Vulnerability scanning is a separate feature offered by Docker Scout, Snyk, Trivy, or registry-native scanners; DCT is a signing framework, not a scanner.

questions.question: A container must run with no external connectivity whatsoever — no DNS, no outbound, no inbound — with only a loopback interface inside. Which network driver satisfies that requirement?
options: The bridge driver with --icc=false, which blocks inter-container traffic on the same bridge
The none driver, which gives the container only a loopback interface and no other links
A driver named 'isolated', which disables ingress on the default network
The host driver, which shares the host's network namespace with the container
questions.explanation: The none driver attaches no interfaces beyond `lo`, so the container cannot reach anything and nothing can reach it — exactly the required air-gapped shape. `--icc=false` only blocks container-to-container traffic on a bridge, leaving external and inbound access intact via NAT and port publishing. There is no built-in driver called `isolated`; that name does not resolve to any of Docker's network drivers. The host driver is the opposite of isolation: the container shares every host interface, so it can reach and be reached across the whole network.

questions.question: A developer edits inside a running container, then runs `docker commit` to create a new image with those changes baked in. Why is `docker commit` discouraged as a production workflow?
options: It silently overwrites the parent image's tag on the local host, making the previous image content irrecoverable once the new snapshot is created
The resulting image is an opaque snapshot with no Dockerfile-in-source-control provenance, so it is not reproducible or reviewable
It automatically merges the container's runtime application logs into an extra persistent layer, inflating the resulting image size significantly
It automatically pushes the newly committed image to the daemon's default registry as soon as the commit finishes, exposing it before any review
questions.explanation: `docker commit` snapshots a container's writable layer into a new image but records no build recipe: no one else can rebuild the same image from source, and code review has nothing to inspect — that is the reason it is discouraged for anything beyond ad-hoc experiments. It does not overwrite the parent tag; commit produces a new image with its own tag. It does not selectively bake logs into a layer — everything in the writable layer is snapshotted, but that is a consequence of committing, not a special log behavior. And it never auto-pushes; a separate `docker push` is required to reach a registry.

questions.question: An admin needs to cap a container at 1.5 CPUs and 512 MB of memory. Which Linux kernel subsystem does Docker use to meter and enforce those resource limits per container?
options: Linux namespaces, which give the container isolated PID, network, mount, and UTS views
seccomp, which filters the set of syscalls that the container's processes are allowed to make
SELinux/AppArmor MAC, which restricts file and process access via mandatory access control
Control groups (cgroups), which meter and enforce CPU, memory, block I/O, and PID limits per process group
questions.explanation: cgroups are the kernel subsystem that measures and constrains CPU shares/quotas, memory, block I/O, PIDs, and network bandwidth per process group; `docker run --cpus=1.5 --memory=512m` translates directly into cgroup settings. Namespaces provide the isolation dimension (separate PID trees, network stacks, mount tables), not the metering dimension. seccomp is a syscall filter and cannot limit CPU or memory usage. SELinux and AppArmor implement mandatory access control over files and syscalls; they do not throttle resources.

questions.question: An operator wants a list of every Docker volume on a host with its driver and name, using a verb consistent with the rest of the Docker CLI. Which command lists volumes?
options: docker volume list
docker volume ls
docker storage ls
docker volumes show
questions.explanation: `docker volume ls` is the canonical subcommand and mirrors the `container ls`, `image ls`, `network ls` pattern used across the CLI. `docker volume list` is not a valid alias — the CLI only accepts `ls`. `docker storage` is not a Docker top-level command; there is no storage object namespace at the CLI. `docker volumes show` is doubly wrong: the object namespace is singular (`volume`), and the verb is `ls`, not `show`.

questions.question: A Dockerfile with eight sequential `RUN apt-get install …` lines is refactored into a single chained `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y … && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`. Why does the chained form yield a substantially smaller image?
options: Docker runs the sub-commands inside a chained RUN in parallel, which unlocks a tighter compression algorithm on the resulting single layer
Each RUN creates a new image layer, so chaining collapses eight layers into one where the apt cache can also be deleted inside the same layer
Chaining triggers a whole-image content-dedup pass at build time that removes duplicate binaries across the image's layers
The layer-count reduction is a Linux-only side effect: the base image transparently switches to a stripped-down variant when chained RUNs are detected
questions.explanation: Every RUN produces a new read-only layer; eight RUNs create eight layers, and any file removed in a later RUN still occupies bytes in an earlier layer. Chaining installs and cleanup into a single RUN keeps the apt lists out of the layer entirely, cutting size sharply. RUN steps do not execute in parallel — BuildKit can parallelize across stages, but not the commands inside a single RUN, and parallelism does not shrink layers. Docker has no whole-image dedup pass across layers; the copy-on-write filesystem shares layers between images but does not de-duplicate files inside a single image. And Linux-only base-image switching is not a real Docker feature.

questions.question: A web container's PID 1 stays alive but the HTTP endpoint returns 500s. Which Dockerfile instruction lets the daemon (and Swarm/Compose) periodically probe the container and mark it unhealthy when the probe fails?
options: A NETWORKCHECK instruction that validates connectivity to the container's published port
The HEALTHCHECK instruction, whose CMD returns exit 0 for healthy and non-zero for unhealthy
A SYNTAXCHECK instruction that validates the Dockerfile at container start
An ENVCHECK instruction that verifies required environment variables are set
questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK defines a command (with configurable interval, timeout, retries, start-period) that Docker runs inside the container; the container's status is set to starting, healthy, or unhealthy based on the exit codes, and Swarm uses that status to replace failing tasks. NETWORKCHECK, SYNTAXCHECK, and ENVCHECK are not real Dockerfile instructions — the parser would reject them. The only container-level runtime health mechanism baked into the image is HEALTHCHECK.

questions.question: A `docker service update` rollout is in progress and new tasks are failing. Without intervention, Swarm keeps replacing healthy old tasks with broken new ones. Which flag pauses the rolling update on failure so the operator can investigate?
options: --failure-action=stop
--update-failure-action=pause
--rollback-on-failure=true
--update-policy=halt
questions.explanation: `--update-failure-action=pause` halts the rolling update when the failure ratio is exceeded, letting the operator triage before more old tasks are replaced; the alternative values are `continue` (default) and `rollback`. `--failure-action` (without `update-`) does not exist for `service update`. `--rollback-on-failure` is not a real flag; automatic rollback is achieved with `--update-failure-action=rollback`, plus the separate `--rollback-*` tuning flags. `--update-policy=halt` is invented — there is no `--update-policy` flag in the Docker CLI.

questions.question: A Swarm service needs a database password. It must be encrypted at rest in the Swarm state and delivered to the container as an in-memory file under `/run/secrets/`, never persisted on disk or bakeable into the image. Which feature meets that requirement?
options: Docker Secrets — encrypted in the Raft log, mounted as tmpfs at /run/secrets in target containers only
Hard-coding the password with an ENV instruction in the Dockerfile at build time
Passing the password as a plain environment variable in the compose file's environment: block
Mounting a host directory that contains a password file into the container as a bind mount
questions.explanation: Docker Secrets store the secret encrypted in Swarm's Raft log, ship it to authorized nodes over mTLS, and expose it inside the container as a tmpfs-backed file at `/run/secrets/<name>` — never on disk on the worker. Hard-coding via ENV bakes the secret into every image layer and is visible through `docker history` and `docker inspect`. Compose-style environment variables travel through the process environment and are readable with `docker inspect`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and many logs. A bind mount from the host keeps the secret in plaintext on every worker's disk and outside Docker's access-controlled distribution mechanism.

questions.question: An operator needs to open an interactive `bash` shell inside a container that is already running, not start a new container. Which command does this?
options: docker exec -it myapp bash
docker shell myapp
docker attach myapp
docker run -it myapp bash
questions.explanation: `docker exec -it <container> bash` spawns a new bash process inside the already-running container: `-i` keeps STDIN open and `-t` allocates a PTY. `docker shell` is not a real subcommand and would be rejected by the CLI. `docker attach` connects the terminal to the container's existing PID 1 rather than starting a shell, so if PID 1 is nginx you just get nginx's stdio, not a shell. `docker run` always starts a brand-new container from the image, which does not satisfy the 'already running container' constraint.

questions.question: A container must bind to port 80 but should not have any other root privileges on the host kernel. What is the recommended least-privilege pattern for that container?
options: Run with --privileged and rely on the seccomp profile to block dangerous syscalls at runtime
Remove AppArmor and seccomp profiles so only capabilities gate what the process can do
Drop all Linux capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL and add back only --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE
Disable networking with --network=none and disable the mount namespace so bind(2) succeeds anyway
questions.explanation: Dropping ALL capabilities and re-adding only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` is the classical least-privilege pattern: the process keeps the exact power it needs (bind to a port below 1024) and nothing else. `--privileged` is the opposite — it disables namespaces, capability dropping, and the default seccomp profile. Removing AppArmor and seccomp weakens the defense-in-depth around capabilities rather than tightening it. Disabling networking with `--network=none` breaks the requirement to serve on port 80, and namespace changes cannot substitute for CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE.

questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the relationship between a Docker registry and Docker Hub?
options: A registry is the server-side storage and distribution system for images; Docker Hub is one specific public registry operated by Docker Inc.
Docker Hub and a Docker registry are two names for the same underlying object; the term used depends on whether you are logged into Docker Inc.'s hosted instance
Docker Hub is the free open-source reference implementation while any other registry is a proprietary commercial product requiring a paid license per pull
A Docker registry stores container runtime logs and traces alongside images, and Docker Hub is specifically the observability side of that stack
questions.explanation: A Docker registry is any service that speaks the Docker Registry HTTP API v2 for storing and serving images; Docker Hub is the specific public registry that Docker Inc. operates. Other registries include ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, Harbor, and self-hosted `registry:2`. Hub and registry are not synonyms — Hub is one registry among many. The reference open-source implementation (`distribution/distribution`) is Apache-2 licensed; commercial and free registries both exist, so the licensing framing is wrong. Registries do not store container logs; log storage is handled by logging drivers or external systems.

questions.question: A team wants to push a local image called `myapp:latest` to their private registry at `registry.company.com`. Which two-step sequence does that correctly?
options: docker rename myapp:latest registry.company.com/myapp:latest && docker upload registry.company.com/myapp:latest
docker tag myapp:latest registry.company.com/myapp:latest && docker push registry.company.com/myapp:latest
docker image publish myapp:latest --to registry.company.com
docker push registry.company.com/myapp:latest by itself, with no earlier tagging step
questions.explanation: Push needs an image reference whose repository is prefixed with the target registry hostname; `docker tag` creates that alias for the existing image ID, and `docker push` then uploads the layers. `docker rename` and `docker upload` are not Docker subcommands. `docker image publish` does not exist either; the CLI verbs for shipping to a registry are `tag` + `push` (with `docker login` for authentication). Running `docker push registry.company.com/myapp:latest` on its own fails because the local image has no such tag yet — no repository/name mapping exists for Docker to send.

questions.question: Which statement most accurately captures the practical difference between a bind mount and a named Docker volume?
options: Docker volumes are strictly read-only inside the container by design; bind mounts are the only mount type that supports read-write access to persistent host data
Bind mounts are available only on Linux hosts; Docker volumes are the only mount type that works on Windows and macOS Docker installations
A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container and is tied to that path; a Docker volume is managed by Docker with its own lifecycle and works with volume drivers
Bind mounts are strictly faster than named Docker volumes because bind-mounted paths bypass Docker's storage stack and hit the host filesystem directly
questions.explanation: The defining distinction is management and portability: a bind mount pins the container to a specific host path, while a Docker volume is created and located by Docker itself and can be backed by pluggable drivers (NFS, EBS, and so on). Read-only vs read-write is orthogonal — both mount types support `:ro` and are read-write by default. Bind mounts work on Windows and macOS hosts (with path translation) and Docker volumes work everywhere too, so the OS-only claim is false. On Linux, both mount types write to a host filesystem with equivalent performance; performance is not a defining bind-vs-volume distinction.

questions.question: A Dockerfile puts `COPY package.json ./` before `RUN npm install` and `COPY . .` afterwards. What behavior of the Docker build cache does this ordering exploit?
options: Docker caches the whole image as a single opaque unit and only rebuilds it when the base image referenced in FROM changes or is repulled
Docker caches RUN instructions but always rebuilds any COPY instruction because file bytes are considered volatile, so ordering does not affect cache reuse
Each instruction is cached individually and a cache miss on any instruction invalidates the cache for that instruction and every subsequent instruction
Docker caches its builds by tag: any change to a Dockerfile is re-cached under a new automatically incremented tag so previous build work is retained under the old tag
questions.explanation: The Docker build cache is per-instruction and sequential: if `COPY package.json` and its inputs are unchanged, `RUN npm install` above it stays cached; but as soon as any instruction (or its inputs) changes, that layer and every subsequent layer are rebuilt. That is exactly why frequently changing content (`COPY . .`) goes near the end. There is no whole-image cache tied only to FROM changes; content of intermediate instructions is what invalidates. COPY steps are cached the same way RUN steps are — Docker hashes the copied file set. And tag-based caching is not how the layer cache works.

questions.question: A Swarm monitoring agent must run exactly one task on every node currently in the cluster and on any node that joins later. Which Swarm service mode achieves that?
options: A federated-service mode that spreads work across separate Swarm clusters
Global mode — the scheduler runs exactly one task on every Active node in the Swarm
An external-IP mode that assigns each node's task a routable public IP
An unlimited-replicas mode that scales freely across all nodes without a target count
questions.explanation: Global-mode services run exactly one task per Active node — as nodes join, tasks are scheduled on them automatically; as nodes leave, their tasks are cleaned up. This is the closest analogue to Kubernetes DaemonSets. There is no federated mode across separate clusters — Swarm has no built-in multi-cluster federation. There is no `external-IP mode`; publishing is controlled via `--publish` on services, not a service mode. `Unlimited replicas` is not a valid mode: services are either replicated (with a fixed replica count) or global.

questions.question: `docker save` and `docker export` both write a tar file, but they capture different things. What is the actual difference?
options: `docker save` uploads the image directly to a remote registry over HTTPS; `docker export` is the equivalent of `save` for producing a local tar archive on disk
The two commands are functionally identical and differ only in their default output filename convention (`image.tar` versus `container.tar`)
`docker save` captures the live memory state of a running container; `docker export` writes the underlying image with all of its ordered layers preserved
`docker save` writes an image (all layers, tags, and metadata); `docker export` writes a container's flattened filesystem with no layer history
questions.explanation: `docker save <image>` produces a tarball of the image — every layer, plus tags and metadata — that can be re-imported with `docker load`. `docker export <container>` writes the container's current filesystem as a flat single-layer tar that can be re-imported with `docker import`, discarding layers, tags, and Dockerfile-time metadata. Neither command talks to a registry (that is `push`). They are not identical, and their subjects are swapped in the third option — `save` operates on images, `export` on containers.

questions.question: A production container has just exited with status 137 (OOM-killed). Which command shows what the application wrote to stdout/stderr before it died?
options: docker container stdout <container>
docker inspect --logs <container>
docker debug <container>
docker logs <container>
questions.explanation: `docker logs <container>` reads the container's stdout/stderr as recorded by the configured logging driver, and it works for containers that are running or already stopped (as long as `--rm` did not delete the container). `docker container stdout` is not a real subcommand. `docker inspect` prints configuration and state JSON but has no `--logs` flag and never returns log lines. `docker debug` is an interactive debug shell (in newer Docker Desktop builds) that starts a debugger container — it is not the way to fetch historical stdout.

questions.question: The USER instruction in a Dockerfile is the canonical way to run a container as a non-root user. What does USER actually do?
options: It sets the user and optional group that subsequent RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions execute as inside the image
It restricts which users on the host system are allowed to run `docker run` against the resulting image
It restricts which registry accounts are allowed to pull the resulting image after it has been pushed
It creates a matching user account on the host system when the image is pulled
questions.explanation: USER changes the user (and optional group) that any subsequent RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions run as, and becomes the default user of the running container. Access to `docker run` on the host is controlled by membership in the `docker` group or by authorization plugins, not by anything inside the image. Registry-side pull access is enforced by the registry's IAM/roles, and Dockerfile instructions cannot influence that. Pulling an image never modifies the host's `/etc/passwd`; USER changes only the image's own metadata.

questions.question: A running container `web` is on the `frontend` network. The admin wants to attach it to a `backend` network as well without stopping and recreating it. Which command does that?
options: docker container network-add web backend
docker run --network=backend web
docker network connect backend web
docker network join backend web
questions.explanation: `docker network connect <network> <container>` attaches an already-running container to an additional network and gives it a new interface and IP on that network; `docker network disconnect` is the inverse. `docker container network-add` is not a real subcommand. `docker run --network=…` sets the network for a brand-new container, not for one that is already running. `docker network join` is not a real subcommand either — the analogous verb (`swarm join`) belongs to the `swarm` object, not `network`.

questions.question: A Swarm with 5 managers loses 3 of them at once. Which statement best describes what happens to the cluster?
options: Losing any single manager immediately halts scheduling and blocks all writes because Raft consensus cannot tolerate the failure of even one voting manager in a 5-node quorum
Worker nodes automatically self-promote to managers whenever Raft quorum is lost, restoring the (N/2)+1 majority within seconds without any operator involvement
In Swarm, managers only run workload tasks while workers handle Raft consensus and scheduling — so with 3 workers still alive the cluster remains fully writable
The remaining managers lack the (N/2)+1 quorum, so no new state changes can be committed — existing tasks keep running but no new services, updates, or scaling operations can succeed
questions.explanation: Raft requires (N/2)+1 managers for a write quorum. With 5 managers configured, quorum is 3; losing 3 leaves 2 healthy managers, so the cluster becomes read-only. Existing tasks keep running because the workers already have their instructions, but no new services, updates, scaling, or node changes can be committed until quorum is restored. The 'single-manager failure halts scheduling' claim is false — 5 managers tolerate 2 failures cleanly. Workers do not auto-promote; promotion is an explicit manager operation and is impossible without quorum. Raft consensus and scheduling live on the managers, not on the workers, so the third option inverts the architecture.

questions.question: A container needs a fast scratch directory that lives entirely in RAM, never touches host disk, and is wiped as soon as the container stops. Which mount type fits?
options: A compressed overlay-filesystem mount over the image's read-only layers
A read-only bind mount from a host directory into the container's scratch path
A tmpfs mount at the scratch path
A persistent BuildKit cache mount that is reused across image builds
questions.explanation: A tmpfs mount is backed by the host's RAM and never lands on disk; when the container stops the tmpfs area is torn down, matching every requirement. An overlay mount over the image layers is the container's normal writable layer — it lives on disk and grows with writes, and it is not addressable as its own mount type in `docker run`. A read-only bind mount cannot serve as scratch space because writes are forbidden. A BuildKit cache mount is a build-time construct, not a runtime container mount, and it deliberately persists across builds.

questions.question: A container must be capped at 256 MB of memory and half a CPU core. Which pair of `docker run` flags achieves that correctly?
options: --memory=256m --cpus=0.5
--mem-limit --cpu-quota=50
--ram=256mb --cpu=half
--memory=256 --cpu-shares=0.5
questions.explanation: `--memory=256m` sets a hard 256 MiB memory cap (container is OOM-killed above it) and `--cpus=0.5` maps to a CPU quota equal to half a core — the canonical modern syntax. `--mem-limit` is not a real flag; the flag is `--memory`. `--ram` and `--cpu=half` are also invented; Docker does not accept English words for CPU fractions. `--memory=256` without a suffix means 256 bytes and would fail validation, and `--cpu-shares` is a relative weight, not an absolute core-fraction cap, so 0.5 there does not produce a half-core limit.

questions.question: An engineer wants to remove not just dangling images but all locally stored images that are not currently used by any container. Which command does that in one call?
options: docker image prune --older-than 24h — removes images older than 24 hours regardless of use
docker image prune — removes only dangling (untagged) image layers
docker image prune -a — removes all unused images including tagged ones
docker image prune --keep-in-use — removes images currently referenced by running containers
questions.explanation: `docker image prune -a` removes every image that is not referenced by at least one container (running or stopped), including tagged ones — exactly the scope the question asks for. Plain `docker image prune` (no `-a`) only removes dangling images with no repo/tag. `--older-than` is not a real flag; the equivalent is `--filter until=24h` and even that leaves tagged-but-unused images behind unless `-a` is present. `--keep-in-use` is invented; images in use are never pruned in any mode, so this option's stated behavior is impossible.

questions.question: A Compose file lists a web service with `depends_on: [db]`. On `docker compose up` the web container starts before Postgres is ready and its connection attempt fails. What does plain `depends_on` actually guarantee?
options: Compose implicitly waits until every dependent service has reported healthy via its HEALTHCHECK block before starting the dependent service, whether or not you added `condition:`
Compose creates a synchronized inter-container network link on `depends_on` that is only opened for reads and writes once both services are simultaneously running and responsive
Compose copies the depended-on service's runtime configuration and environment variables into the dependent container's environment before the dependent container's process starts
Compose only orders startup: web starts after db's container starts, but not after db is ready to accept traffic
questions.explanation: Plain `depends_on` controls startup and shutdown order only — `web` is started after `db`'s container has been created, but Compose does not wait for anything inside `db` to be ready. Waiting for readiness requires the extended form `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy` combined with a HEALTHCHECK on `db`. There is no synchronized-network-link primitive tied to `depends_on`. Compose does not copy one service's configuration into another as part of `depends_on`; that would require explicit `environment` or `env_file` wiring.

questions.question: A Dockerfile has `EXPOSE 80`. After `docker run myimage`, port 80 is not reachable from the host. Which statement correctly describes what EXPOSE does?
options: EXPOSE writes the listed ports into the daemon's iptables/nftables allow list so inbound host firewall traffic is permitted on those ports for every run of the image
EXPOSE opens the listed container ports and publishes each of them to a randomly assigned host port whenever `docker run` starts a container from the image
EXPOSE only documents which ports the container listens on — it does not publish anything; `-p` or `-P` on docker run does the actual publishing
EXPOSE forwards the container's environment variables to the host process listening on the listed ports so external tools can read them without inspecting the container
questions.explanation: EXPOSE is metadata: it tells humans and tools which ports the container process is expected to listen on, and it also acts as the port list that `docker run -P` uses when auto-publishing to random host ports. It does not by itself publish, NAT, or allow anything. It does not touch the host firewall — that is either kept out of the picture or handled by iptables rules Docker installs when you actually publish a port. `-P` (capital) publishes exposed ports to random host ports at run time; that behavior belongs to `-P`, not to EXPOSE alone. And EXPOSE has nothing to do with environment variables.

questions.question: A container sees its own PID 1, its own network interfaces, its own filesystem root, and its own hostname — separate from the host's. Which Linux kernel feature provides those isolated views?
options: Control groups (cgroups v1/v2), which meter and enforce CPU shares and quotas, memory ceilings, block I/O, and PID counts per container process group
AppArmor, which applies per-process mandatory access control policies over file paths and syscalls and can restrict what a container's processes may open
seccomp (secure computing mode), which filters the set of Linux syscalls that a process is allowed to make and is applied by Docker via a default profile
Linux namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP), which give each container its own view of kernel resources
questions.explanation: Namespaces are the kernel primitive that produces isolated views: PID namespace for process IDs, NET namespace for network stacks, MNT namespace for filesystem mounts, UTS for hostname, IPC for shared memory, USER for UID mapping. cgroups do resource metering and enforcement, not isolation — they answer 'how much', not 'what can I see'. AppArmor is a Linux MAC layer for files and syscalls; it does not create isolated PID trees or network stacks. seccomp filters syscalls but does not give a process its own PID tree, network stack, or filesystem root.

questions.question: A Swarm service needs an environment-specific nginx.conf that differs between dev, staging, and prod. The file is not sensitive but should be managed centrally in Swarm and mounted into the container as a file — without rebuilding the image. Which Swarm feature fits?
options: An NFS bind mount populated by a Puppet run on each Swarm node
An ENV instruction in the Dockerfile that inlines the config text at build time
Docker Configs — non-sensitive configuration objects stored in Swarm and mounted as files at a target path in each task
Per-environment images tagged nginx:dev, nginx:staging, nginx:prod that each embed the appropriate config
questions.explanation: Docker Configs are the direct answer: `docker config create` stores the file in the Swarm's Raft log, and `docker service create --config source=...,target=...` mounts it inside each task at the chosen path, exactly like Secrets but without encryption. NFS bind mounts can also work but are managed outside Swarm and impose external infrastructure. Baking config into ENV at build time couples config changes to image rebuilds and does not deliver a file, which the requirement calls for. Per-environment images are an anti-pattern: they diverge from the immutable-image-with-external-config principle and defeat the point of one image per binary.

questions.question: A defense-in-depth pattern runs a container with its root filesystem mounted read-only; the app writes only to tmpfs and volumes. Which `docker run` flag enables that?
options: --read-only, which makes the container's root filesystem read-only
--image-read-only, which pins the source image to a read-only registry copy
--isolate-writes, which prevents other containers from reading this container's filesystem
--config-immutable, which prevents runtime changes to the container's configuration
questions.explanation: `docker run --read-only` mounts the container's rootfs read-only; combine with `--tmpfs /tmp` (and named volumes for real state) so the app still has writable scratch and persistent storage. It hardens the container against write-based persistence and log tampering after an intrusion. `--image-read-only` is invented — images in the local content store are already immutable and Docker has no such flag. `--isolate-writes` and `--config-immutable` are also invented flags. The specific defense-in-depth pattern in the question maps directly to `--read-only`.

questions.question: An ops engineer wants a live, top-like view of every running container's CPU%, memory usage against its limit, network I/O, and block I/O. Which command provides that?
options: docker container metrics
docker top <container>
docker stats
docker inspect <container>
questions.explanation: `docker stats` streams live CPU%, memory usage/limit, net I/O, block I/O, and PID counts for every running container until interrupted; `--no-stream` gives a single snapshot for scripts. `docker container metrics` is not a real command. `docker top <container>` runs `ps` inside a single container and lists processes, not resource stats. `docker inspect` returns static configuration JSON — mount paths, network, entrypoint — but no live resource metrics.

questions.question: A Dockerfile needs to declare a variable that is available both during subsequent RUN steps in the build and inside the running container process at runtime. Which instruction does that?
options: ARG
VARIABLE
SET
ENV
questions.explanation: ENV sets an environment variable in the image config so it is present during subsequent build steps AND in the container's process environment at runtime. ARG sets a build-time variable only and is not visible to the running container unless it is copied into an ENV. VARIABLE and SET are not real Dockerfile instructions — the parser rejects both. Also worth remembering: because ENV values are visible via `docker inspect`, they must never be used for secrets.

questions.question: An admin needs to copy `/var/log/app.log` from a running container `web` to a local `./logs/` directory in one command. Which command does that directly?
options: docker transfer web:/var/log/app.log ./logs/
docker pull web:/var/log/app.log
docker export web > ./logs/app.log
docker cp web:/var/log/app.log ./logs/
questions.explanation: `docker cp` copies files between the host filesystem and a container in either direction, with container paths written as `<container>:<path>` — exactly the operation requested. `docker transfer` is not a real subcommand. `docker pull` fetches images from a registry; it cannot address a file inside a container. `docker export` writes the container's entire filesystem as a tarball to stdout, not a single file — you would end up with a tar of the whole container renamed to `app.log`, not the log file itself.

questions.question: Which statement most accurately captures the difference between exec form and shell form for ENTRYPOINT/CMD?
options: The two forms are functionally identical at container-start time and Docker's runtime picks one at random on each `docker run`, so the choice never affects signal handling in practice
Exec form is the JSON-array syntax and runs the executable directly as PID 1; shell form is wrapped in `/bin/sh -c`, which becomes PID 1 and may not forward signals to the actual process
Shell form is the preferred form for production images because the wrapping shell inherits the host's PATH and job-control features and improves graceful-shutdown behaviour on SIGTERM
Exec form requires an absolute path to the binary and skips PATH resolution entirely, whereas shell form is the only form that resolves the command name through the container's `$PATH`
questions.explanation: Exec form (`["python", "app.py"]`) runs the executable as PID 1, so signals like SIGTERM go directly to the app and graceful shutdown works. Shell form (`python app.py`) is silently wrapped in `/bin/sh -c`, making `sh` PID 1; unless the shell forwards signals (many don't), the app never sees SIGTERM. The two forms are not identical and are chosen deterministically by the syntax used. Shell form is not the recommended production form — it is what causes the notorious 'container ignores docker stop' problem. And exec form does resolve through PATH; the absolute-path requirement does not exist.

questions.question: In Docker Swarm, the default ingress overlay network enables the routing mesh. Which statement best describes what that means?
options: Any Swarm node accepts connections on a service's published port and routes them via ingress+IPVS to a healthy task, regardless of which node the task runs on
It is the manager control-plane Raft overlay that carries manager-to-manager consensus traffic between Swarm managers and is disabled on worker nodes by default
It is a dedicated metrics-collection overlay that carries container health and telemetry data from every worker node up to the Swarm managers for aggregation
It is an external load-balancer integration overlay that offloads all L4 load balancing for published ports to a configured cloud provider's managed LB
questions.explanation: The ingress network is what makes the Swarm routing mesh work: every node listens on each service's published port and, if the local node has no task for that service, forwards the connection over the ingress overlay + IPVS to a node that does. That is why a single external load balancer can point at any Swarm node IP. Raft traffic between managers rides a separate control-plane connection, not the ingress overlay. There is no metrics-collection overlay by design in Swarm — metrics ride whatever telemetry driver you plug in. And ingress is not an external LB integration; it is an internal, in-cluster L4 load balancer built on IPVS.

questions.question: An admin wants a per-layer report for an image: which instruction created each layer, when, and how many bytes it added. Which command emits that?
options: docker layer list <image>
docker image inspect --layers <image>
docker image layers --verbose <image>
docker image history <image>
questions.explanation: `docker image history <image>` lists the layers of an image in order, showing the creating command, creation time, and size, and is the standard tool for spotting which Dockerfile instruction ballooned the image. `docker layer list` and `docker image layers` are not real subcommands. `docker image inspect` returns configuration JSON but does not accept `--layers` and does not produce a per-layer size breakdown; the RootFS section only lists layer digests, without sizes or creating commands.

questions.question: A Swarm admin runs `docker node update --availability drain <node>`. What happens to that node's tasks and its role in future scheduling?
options: Tasks on the drained node are terminated immediately and are not rescheduled anywhere else, so the service's replica count drops for the duration of the drain
The node is permanently removed from the Swarm inventory the moment drain is applied and must be re-joined with a freshly issued worker token to become eligible again
Existing tasks keep running on the node in their current state, but new tasks are blocked from being scheduled on it while its availability remains drain
Existing tasks are stopped and rescheduled onto other Active nodes, and no new tasks are scheduled on the drained node until it is set Active again
questions.explanation: `--availability=drain` gracefully evicts a node: its running tasks are stopped and Swarm places replacements on other Active nodes, while no new tasks are scheduled there until the node is set back to `active`. This is the intended pattern for taking a node out for patching or reboot. Tasks are not simply terminated without replacement — the replica count is preserved. The node is not removed from the Swarm (that is `docker node rm`), it just becomes ineligible for new tasks. And 'existing tasks keep running while new ones are blocked' describes the `pause` availability, not `drain`.

questions.question: Docker applies a default seccomp profile to every container. Which of the following best describes what seccomp does?
options: It encrypts inter-container traffic on overlay networks between Swarm nodes
It restricts which Linux syscalls a container's processes are allowed to invoke
It restricts which Docker CLI commands each host user is authorized to run
It rate-limits the container's network bandwidth and shapes egress QoS
questions.explanation: seccomp (secure computing mode) is a kernel syscall filter; Docker's default profile blocks about 44 dangerous syscalls (like `kexec_load`, `reboot`, `add_key`) and allows the rest, and custom profiles can tighten it further. Encrypting overlay traffic is done with `--opt encrypted` on the overlay network, unrelated to seccomp. Restricting CLI commands per host user is the job of Docker authorization plugins (via `--authorization-plugin`), not seccomp. Network bandwidth shaping is handled by cgroups and tc; seccomp filters syscalls and has no bandwidth knob.

questions.question: A Swarm service running `myapp:1.4` at 5 replicas needs a zero-downtime rolling update to `myapp:1.5`. Which command performs that?
options: docker service restart webapp --image myapp:1.5
docker service update --image myapp:1.5 webapp
docker service redeploy webapp --tag 1.5
docker swarm update --image myapp:1.5 webapp
questions.explanation: `docker service update --image myapp:1.5 webapp` triggers a rolling update using the service's configured update policy (`--update-parallelism`, `--update-delay`, `--update-failure-action`, and health checks), which is the recommended zero-downtime pattern. `docker service restart` is not a real subcommand. `docker service redeploy` does not exist. `docker swarm update` does exist but manages Swarm-wide settings (join tokens, cert rotation), not per-service images.

questions.question: BuildKit is Docker's modern build engine (default in current Docker versions and enabled by `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` on older ones). Which of the following statements best describes BuildKit?
options: BuildKit is Docker's replacement for Docker Compose as the runtime orchestrator for multi-container applications; it can execute a docker-compose.yml file directly against a single host without any Compose binary installed, and picks up service definitions automatically

BuildKit runs only on Windows Server hosts and is used exclusively for building Windows-based container images from Dockerfiles that begin with `FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/*`; on Linux hosts the legacy builder is still the only supported build subsystem

BuildKit is a commercial-only add-on shipped with Docker Business and Docker Enterprise; it requires a per-builder-node paid license to unlock its concurrent build steps, cache mounts, and secret and SSH mount features on Linux and Windows

BuildKit is Docker's newer build subsystem, adding parallel build steps, per-stage caching, `RUN --mount=type=secret` and `type=ssh`, cross-platform builds via `--platform`, and shared caches via `RUN --mount=type=cache`
questions.explanation: BuildKit is the modern build subsystem (LLB-based) shipped with Docker; its notable features are exactly the ones listed: parallel steps across stages, better caching, build-time secret and SSH mounts that never persist into layers, cross-platform builds via `--platform`, and reusable cache mounts. It has nothing to do with orchestrating containers — that is Compose/Swarm's job. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows hosts and builds both Linux and Windows images. It is open source and free; no paid Docker EE license is required to use it.

questions.question: A Dockerfile sets `WORKDIR /app`. What does that instruction do?
options: It sets the working directory for subsequent RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, and ADD instructions, creating the directory if it does not already exist
It sets the working directory on the Docker host from which subsequent COPY and ADD instructions read files, effectively redefining the build context root
It specifies the host path where Docker stores its build-layer cache for subsequent multi-stage build stages of this Dockerfile in the daemon's graph driver
It bind-mounts the specified host directory into the intermediate build container at build time so subsequent COPY and ADD instructions can read directly from it
questions.explanation: WORKDIR sets the current directory for all subsequent build instructions and becomes the container's default working directory, and it creates the path if missing. The source directory for COPY/ADD is the build context (implicit `PWD` at build time), not WORKDIR. The layer cache lives under Docker's storage graph (for example `/var/lib/docker/buildkit/`), and WORKDIR has no bearing on where it is stored. WORKDIR is not a bind mount either — nothing from the host is mounted; the source of COPY/ADD is the build context tar.

questions.question: A team wants Docker volumes to be backed by external storage such as AWS EBS, Azure Disk, S3, or NFS, so `docker volume create --driver <plugin> …` provisions storage in that system. Which Docker plugin category enables that?
options: Authorization plugins, which gate the Docker CLI based on user identity and request policies
Volume plugins (volume drivers), which expose external or cloud storage as Docker volumes
Logging plugins, which forward container stdout/stderr to external log sinks
Network plugins, which provide custom network drivers for container connectivity
questions.explanation: Volume plugins (volume drivers) are the extension point Docker exposes for pluggable storage back-ends: examples include REX-Ray for EBS/S3/Azure Disk/GCE PD, Portworx, and various NFS drivers. Once installed, `docker volume create --driver <plugin>` provisions the underlying storage. Authorization plugins gate CLI access via the daemon's authz interface — they cannot supply storage. Logging plugins deal with stdout/stderr forwarding, not persistent volumes. Network plugins provide network drivers such as Weave or Calico, not volume back-ends.

questions.question: A Dockerfile must accept a build-time value via `docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.2.3 …`, consumed by `RUN echo $VERSION > /etc/version.txt`, and must NOT persist that value into the runtime environment. Which instruction declares such a variable?
options: ENV VERSION=1.0
ARG VERSION
BUILD_ARG VERSION
PARAM VERSION
questions.explanation: ARG defines a build-time variable that can be supplied on the CLI via `--build-arg` and is available only during the build — it is not persisted into the container's runtime environment (unless the Dockerfile explicitly copies it into an ENV). ENV would persist the value at runtime, which the requirement forbids. BUILD_ARG and PARAM are not real Dockerfile instructions and the parser rejects them. Because ARG values do show up in `docker history`, secrets should still go through BuildKit's `RUN --mount=type=secret` rather than ARG.

questions.question: An admin runs `docker network inspect mynet`. By design, which fields does the JSON output include for that network?
options: A firewall-rules summary produced by parsing the host's active iptables/nftables tables and grouping the rules that reference the network's bridge interface
Real-time traffic statistics such as bytes and packets in and out over the last minute, broken down per attached container and per direction
Only DNS server configuration for the network, including the embedded resolver IP, upstream forwarders, and any per-container aliases registered in the network
Network metadata — id/name/driver/scope, IPAM subnet and gateway, options and labels, and a Containers map of connected containers with their IPs
questions.explanation: `docker network inspect` returns configuration and membership data: id, name, driver, scope, IPAM subnet and gateway, options, labels, and a Containers section that maps attached containers to their IPs and endpoints. It does not produce a firewall summary — Docker installs iptables rules but the network inspect output does not summarize them. It is not a real-time traffic meter; live stats live in `docker stats` or external tooling. And it exposes far more than DNS config — DNS configuration is not even a first-class field on user-defined bridges.

questions.question: Swarm managers use Raft consensus, which needs a majority of managers to commit state changes. For production, you want the smallest cluster that tolerates exactly one manager failure. How many managers should you run?
options: 2 managers
5 managers
3 managers
1 manager
questions.explanation: With 3 managers, the Raft quorum is 2; that tolerates exactly one manager failure and is the recommended minimum for production. The formula is `2F+1` managers to tolerate F failures, so 3 → 1, 5 → 2, 7 → 3. 2 managers is strictly worse than 1: quorum is still 2, so any single failure loses quorum, and you also double the split-brain surface. 5 managers works but exceeds the 'smallest cluster tolerating one failure' requirement — it tolerates two. 1 manager tolerates zero failures and is not a production configuration.

questions.question: During a Dockerfile build, some instructions add a new image layer (a diff in the union filesystem) while others only modify the image config. Which TWO instructions create a new image LAYER?
options: RUN — executes a command and writes the resulting filesystem changes as a new layer
COPY (and ADD) — copies source files into the image, producing a new layer with the new files
ENV — sets an environment variable in the image config; metadata only, no filesystem layer
LABEL — adds a key/value label to the image config; metadata only, no filesystem layer
questions.explanation: RUN and COPY/ADD are the filesystem-modifying instructions and each produces a new content layer. ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE, USER, WORKDIR, ARG, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT all update the image config or metadata without touching the filesystem, so no new content layer is created. BuildKit may reorganize some of these under the hood, but conceptually the DCA exam distinguishes layer-producing from metadata-only instructions along exactly this line.
